Skunk Works · SKW-033 · State of play, July 2026

The wagon is one folded sheet.

No tube frame. No fabric bag. No fasteners. The creases are the hinges and the folded sheet is the structure — a wagon body that packs to briefcase thickness and opens in one motion.

Westfield Outdoors · Industrial Design

01 — The problem

Folding wagons haven't changed in a decade.

Every folding wagon on the shelf is the same machine: a steel tube frame with a fabric bag hung inside it. They differ in colour and cupholders. The frame is what folds — so the collapsed size is set by the tubes, and the fabric just goes along for the ride.

  • 01Bulky collapsed profile. You fold the frame, not the volume. Quad-fold and bi-fold both leave a long, heavy bundle.
  • 02Setup fights the user. Multi-step deployment, pinch points, and a bag that has to be re-seated every time.
  • 03Visually homogeneous. Nothing on the shelf differentiates one from the next, so the category competes on price.
01 — The problem

02 — The insight

Make the basket the structure.

Living hinges plus origami. One sheet of polymer, scored with an engineered crease pattern, folds into a rigid basket and collapses flat. The part that carries the load and the part that folds are the same part.

There is no frame to fold around, so the collapsed size is set by the material stack instead of by tube diameter. That is where the compactness comes from — and it is not an increment on the existing category, it is a different machine.

4.0″collapsed body

02 — The insight

03 — Why this is a skunk works project

A category with no competition — if the mechanism survives.

The payoff

  • ◆Establishes a new product category with no immediate competitor.
  • ◆Fewer parts than tube-and-fabric: one moulded body replaces frame, bag, and fasteners.
  • ◆Mono-material and recyclable — a real sustainability story, not a claim.
  • ◆Flat-pack shipping and retail display; strong IP position on geometry and process.

The chartered risk

  • ▲The mechanism may not function at full scale, or may not be durable enough for outdoor use.
  • ▲Living hinges have to survive hundreds of fold cycles without cracking.
  • ▲Tooling for a body this size is a significant commitment to make on a hunch.

Everything since March has been about retiring that one risk.

04 — The road so far

05 — The obstacle

The one-third-scale sample raised three problems. One of them threatened the concept itself.

“The bottom surface becomes a series of folds rather than a flat load-bearing plane. This creates a very uneven and wavy bottom, which feels unusual for a cart.”

Wavy floor

“Without any supporting structure, the top edge collapses inward. A reinforcement solution would be needed depending on the intended use scenario.”

Rim collapse

“Because the target load is 50 kg, the lay-up has to be quite thick, which makes the folds harder and increases the folding volume. This directly conflicts with the accordion-style folding concept.”

Load vs fold — and: does it really need to be 50 kg?

Stiff enough to carry 50 kg, thin enough to fold flat. If those two genuinely conflict, the concept does not survive a real load.

05 — The obstacle

06 — The approach

So we stopped guessing and solved it.

The CAD was rebuilt as a mathematical machine — 26 rigid panels joined at their creases — and folded numerically from flat sheet to stowed bundle. Seven phases, from CAD intake through to a cut-ready tooling package.

Every number that follows comes out of that model, not out of a sample. The mechanism is real: one degree of freedom, and the deployed CAD geometry sits exactly on the fold path.

06 — The approach

07 — Findings

Three things no further sample would have told us.

The limit

It jams before it lies flat

Past the deployed state both walls lean in over the floor, and their widths sum 44% more than the floor is wide. The opposing rims collide while the bundle is still 216 mm thick.

And the jam is nearly free: under 1 N to bow the walls past each other, at 0.04% strain. It is a rubbing detail, not a blocker — and it explains why the hand sample only “folds after breaking it in”.

The load path

One locked angle makes it rigid

The free basket has three ways to move. Clamp the end angle at both shells and it has none — the whole body goes kinematically rigid from a single control.

Leave one end unlocked at 50 kg and the basket folds off that end: 756 mm of travel. The end lock is not a convenience feature, it is the load path.

Where stiffness goes

The walls are the beam

Deployed, the basket is a folded-plate beam spanning between the two locked shells, and the walls are its webs. They carry about 88% of the bending energy.

Stiffening the floor does nothing at all for sag. Every gram of stiffening belongs on the wall panels.

07 — Findings

08 — The answer

The conflict was never real.

That concern was well founded — a thicker sheet does fight folding. But the model shows the load never needed a thicker sheet — it needed stiffer walls. Ribs on the wall panels alone, floor left bare, take sag at 50 kg from 101 mm down to 5.5 mm.

And they cost almost nothing in folded volume, because ribs nest into each other where added thickness would simply stack — 26 layers deep, in the corners.

Stiffness comes from geometry, not thickness. The 50 kg requirement stands.

Concern raisedWhat the model saysWhat we do
Wavy, non-flat floor Floor stiffness has no measurable effect on sag — the floor is not the structure. Leave it bare; flatness is a finish decision, not a structural one
Top edge collapses inward Reproduced exactly: 100 N inward moved the mid-rim 68 mm. Wall ribs + moulded rim bead → 11.7 mm, fully elastic
50 kg forces a thick lay-up False trade. Wall ribs at 10× bare-sheet stiffness cost +22% mass and no meaningful stack. 5.5 mm sag at 50 kg, 4.0″ bundle — both, not either
Only folds once broken in The rim jam at 75.2°, and it takes under 1 N to pass through it. Engineer the squeeze; no fatigue consequence

It is already drawn.

  • 02Hinge webs ≤ 0.4 mm, 0.2 mm target — set by scoring depth
  • 03Walls-only nested ribs, 5.8 × 2 mm at 25 mm pitch

  • 05No arms — the sheet and the lock carry everything

09 — The package

10 — Where this goes

We can now answer questions about this wagon without cutting material.

That is the real shift. The concept came in as a promising shape that folded when you coaxed it. It now has a solved mechanism, a named load path, a rib architecture, and a tooling file — and the objection that could have ended it turned out to be a false trade.

What changed since April

  • →SRPP lay-up → moulded plastic with ribbed walls
  • →Corner posts lock the basket → one locked end angle does
  • →“About 3 inches” collapsed → 4.0″, accounted layer by layer
  • →Hope it survives 50 kg → 5.5 mm predicted sag

Next three moves

  • 01Send the v1 package to Adam and HF.

  • 03Run the acceptance plan: hinge fatigue, wall coupons, lock proof load, 500 fold cycles at 50 kg.
